questions: Why do you believe what you believe, and could you explain it to a friend?
Peter ran from the cross, then spoke boldly in Acts. What changed him?
Is there a question about your faith you have never felt safe asking?
takeaways: Apologetics means giving a reason, a defense, for the hope you have.
You are called not only to defend your faith but to be able to do it.
Jesus, Paul, and Peter all gave good, consistent reasons for their faith.
challenges: Write down, in your own words, one honest reason you believe.
Read 1 Peter 3:15 this week and notice the words gentleness and respect.
Bring one hard faith question to club and work through it with your group.

questions: When has a friend earned your trust, and what did they do to earn it?
Is the faith you have really your own, or is it borrowed from your parents?
Why do you think Jesus kept his wounds and showed them to Thomas?
takeaways: Biblical faith is trust based on evidence, not wandering in the dark.
John wrote down Jesus' signs so that you may believe (John 20:30-31).
Faith is a solid foundation, like a basement that holds up the whole house.
challenges: Look up Jesus' signs in John's gospel, from water into wine to Lazarus.
Ask yourself honestly whether you have looked at the evidence for Jesus.
Notice this week how trust grows as you get to know a friend better.

questions: Where do you see feelings treated as more important than facts?
Is your favorite ice cream flavor a subjective or an objective truth? Why?
Jesus said 'I am the way.' Can that be true for you but not for others?
takeaways: Truth is what corresponds with reality, whether we like it or not.
Subjective truth is about you; objective truth is about the object.
Jesus' claim in John 14 is objective: true or false, whatever we think.
challenges: Notice one idea this week that sounds good but does not match reality.
Sort three things you believe into subjective truth or objective truth.
Think about how living by what is true could make you more free in Christ.

questions: Should faith make sense? Why or why not?
How do you use logic in your friendships to figure out what's true?
Which argument against Christianity sounds good until you think it through?
takeaways: Logic is not a threat to faith; it is a God-given tool for finding truth.
In Matthew 22 Jesus used careful reasoning to answer the Pharisees.
Maturity means leaving spiritual milk for solid food (Hebrews 5-6).
challenges: Write down one thing about your faith that doesn't make sense to you yet.
When you hear a weak argument, follow it to its natural conclusion.
Read how Paul reasons from Scripture in Acts and notice his logic.

questions: What lenses do you look through, and where did you first pick them up?
Where is your worldview a buffet, with pieces that don't fit together?
How do movies and music you love show a worldview without ever saying so?
takeaways: A worldview is the lens you see through, and it shapes how you live.
A worldview has to be coherent and consistent, or over time it breaks down.
Christianity is compelling because it holds together as one whole view.
challenges: Answer the four worldview questions honestly, not how you think you should.
Notice the worldview behind one show or song you take in this week.
Next time you ask Google a big question, stop and consider the source.

questions: What changes when you know God by name, not just as God Almighty?
How would one personal God change what you believe about right and wrong?
How would one caring, personal God change how you treat friends and family?
takeaways: Monotheism means one personal God who has made himself known to us.
In Exodus 6, God reveals his name, the Lord, and remembers his covenant.
God does not create and walk away; he pursues his people to redeem them.
challenges: Read Exodus 6:1-5 and notice how God describes himself to Moses.
Try viewing one ordinary day as if God is pursuing you personally.
Name one way your view of God could shape culture, not just follow it.

questions: How is God's Spirit living in you different from god being in everything?
Why does it matter that God is distinct from the world He made?
How can you talk about a friend's beliefs honestly and still show love?
takeaways: Pantheism says god is in everything, so nothing is distinct from god.
Losing the line between Creator and creation leads straight to idolatry.
Because God is holy and other than us, we have a standard for right and wrong.
challenges: Notice one place this week where karma, the Force, or yoga shows up.
Read Paul's talk at Mars Hill and spot how he separates God from creation.
Ask yourself what you tend to elevate to god-like status, and why.

questions: Where do you see naturalism showing up in your school or classes?
If only what you can sense is real, where do justice and love come from?
Why would someone who rejects God still want to give kids clean water?
takeaways: Naturalism says only what you can taste, touch, smell, or feel is real.
Science only studies the natural world, so it cannot say why we are here.
Justice, love, and morality point to a Creator beyond the natural world.
challenges: Read the opening of Ecclesiastes and ask what makes your life meaningful.
Notice one moment this week when you are taught that only nature is real.
Ask yourself if what you value and what you believe actually fit together.

questions: Where have you been told that faith and science just don't mix?
What are you learning in school right now that makes you think about God?
Is your faith kept private, or does it show up at school and in public?
takeaways: Science doesn't contradict faith; it lays a foundation to know our world.
The more we discover through science, the more we see how awesome God is.
Faith and science were never meant to live in two separate spheres of life.
challenges: Bring one thing from a science or math class and ask how it points to God.
Ask a Christian who works in science how they see God through their work.
Pick one place where Jesus stays private and let Him into your public life.

questions: If you had no Bible, what would nature alone tell you about God?
Is the universe random chance or a crafted design? Why do you think so?
What does a fine-tuned home for us reveal about God's heart?
takeaways: Like a bottle flip, what looks like luck is really fine-tuning.
Earth's rotation, atmosphere, and distance from the sun are set just so.
God did not just make a habitable planet; He made us a home with love.
challenges: Take one minute this week to consider that God made a place for you.
Notice one thing in nature that seems set just right for life to thrive.
Start putting the pieces together: how does science further your faith?

questions: Halfway through the science unit, what has truly made sense to you so far?
Do you ever nod along in a lesson while secretly thinking you don't get it?
How does comparing DNA to a book help you picture what DNA really is?
takeaways: Honest questions are welcome here; faith grows when you ask them out loud.
What textbooks teach is a narrative you can examine, not just accept.
It is okay to slow down and revisit an idea until it truly makes sense.
challenges: Tell a leader honestly where you are: confused, fired up, or in between.
Notice how your school textbook talks about DNA and bring one line to club.
Try explaining DNA to a friend using the simple picture of a book.

questions: Of fine-tuning, DNA, and design, which evidence spoke to you most, and why?
Was this enough evidence for you, or what questions do you still have?
How can you challenge a teacher's view while still showing real respect?
takeaways: Science is a foundation for understanding our world, not an enemy of faith.
Fine-tuning, DNA, and design all point to God through what science shows.
Know what you believe and why, then share it with love and humility.
challenges: Write down one question about creation or design you still want answered.
Before you debate anyone, check that truth and love are driving you.
Stay patient and keep learning; there is so much more to discover.

questions: Is it a fact that murder is wrong, or just an opinion? How do you know?
Where do your ideas about right and wrong actually come from?
If copying homework isn't wrong just "because we don't," is that a good reason?
takeaways: Right and wrong are more than opinion; God is the standard we compare to.
A boy who is "one Johnny tall" can't measure himself, and neither can we.
Having a sense of right and wrong at all is evidence that points to God.
challenges: Notice one time this week you call something wrong, and ask yourself why.
Ask a friend whether murder is wrong as fact or opinion, and really listen.
Hear someone's reasons fully before you challenge what they believe.

questions: Where do you notice beauty in everyday life, and what might it point to?
Which question from this study is still unanswered for you right now?
How have your beliefs or questions changed since this study began?
takeaways: Beauty, agency, and story point to God, just as morality does.
God is present in the ordinary things you see and interact with every day.
This whole study is meant to prepare you to move the gospel forward.
challenges: Write down one question you feel stuck on and ask a leader this week.
If you're not buying something, say so; honest pushback is welcome here.
Welcome someone new to the group so they don't feel behind or intimidated.

questions: Why do so many questions about why things happen come down to human choices?
Why might the fact that you can choose at all point to a God who exists?
When is it hard to be honest in your group, and what would make it safer?
takeaways: Your ability to choose is a gift from God, and it points to him.
Free will is both a privilege and a responsibility, not just freedom.
How you choose to live should reflect who God is.
challenges: Before each choice this week, big or small, ask if it reflects who God is.
Find one way to serve alongside your group, at church or in your community.
Notice a quiet person in your group and invite them into the conversation.

questions: Where do you see God's rescue or redemption in your own life story?
Why do you think people everywhere love telling and hearing stories?
Which topic this year has been hardest for you to understand or accept?
takeaways: Story itself comes from God, so our love of stories points back to him.
We can tell great stories because we are made in God's image.
Many favorite books and movies carry hidden themes of salvation.
challenges: Watch a movie or read a book this week and look for its redemptive themes.
Pick one topic from this year and explain it to a friend or family member.
Ask a leader one question you still can't answer, or research it yourself.

questions: What is the most improbable event you can think of in human history?
Is a good parking spot or a baby's birth a miracle like those in Scripture?
If miracles still happen, why do you think you rarely see them near you?
takeaways: Miracles point to the fact that God exists and show us exactly who He is.
Science cannot explain the supernatural, so it can't explain away miracles.
God still has the power to do miracles of biblical size if He chooses.
challenges: Read 1 Kings 18 and notice how the fire showed God's sovereign power.
Ask someone you trust whether they have ever witnessed a real miracle.
Be honest with yourself: are you convinced miracles are even possible?

questions: How would you respond to a friend who says the resurrection is just a myth?
How do you know Alexander the Great was real when you weren't there?
Does the evidence convince you Jesus rose, or does something hold you back?
takeaways: Without the resurrection, Christianity falls apart (1 Corinthians 15).
The resurrection is history, with evidence inside and outside the Bible.
No rival theory has better evidence than the resurrection.
challenges: Read 1 Corinthians 15 and notice how Paul points to living witnesses.
Write down one question about the resurrection you still want answered.
If you believe Jesus rose, name one thing in your life that should change.

questions: When Jesus asks 'Who do you say I am?', how would you answer him today?
Why is it easier to call Jesus a good teacher than to call him God?
What evidence backs up who you say you are, and what backs up who Jesus is?
takeaways: In John 8 Jesus flatly claims to be God: 'Before Abraham was born, I am.'
Not everyone who says 'Jesus' means the same thing, so be clear who he is.
A good moral teacher can be ignored, but the God of the universe cannot.
challenges: Read John 8 this week and notice how Jesus describes himself.
Ask a friend who they think Jesus is, then listen for why they think it.
Be honest with yourself: is it a lack of evidence or a lack of willingness?

questions: How would you describe the apostles' conviction, and do you agree with it?
If you knew something was true, how far would you go to make it known?
What does the apostles' fate mean for your own faith, here and now?
takeaways: The apostles lived with Jesus and saw him die and rise with their own eyes.
Nobody dies for what they know is a lie, so the apostles were not lying.
Peter and John could not stop telling what they saw and heard (Acts 4:20).
challenges: Notice one place this week where following Jesus is harder than at club.
Pray for boldness to talk about Jesus where it is not easy or popular.
Review miracles and the resurrection, then ask what changes for you now.

questions: Why does 'the Bible is true because it says so' just go in a circle?
How would you answer a friend who says we only have error-filled copies?
If the Bible really is reliable, what should change in your life this week?
takeaways: No originals of ancient texts survive, only copies called manuscripts.
Over 6,000 New Testament copies agree more than 95 percent of the time.
The New Testament is more reliable than the history in your textbooks.
challenges: List the documents that prove who you are, then ask what proves the Bible.
When a TV expert says the Bible is full of errors, ask for the evidence.
Read something Paul wrote this week, trusting it is what he actually wrote.

questions: How does linking a story to a real object change how much you trust it?
After two weeks of evidence, has the way you see the Bible changed at all?
If a friend said the Bible is just old myths, how would you answer them?
takeaways: The Bible is God's inspired Word, and it is also real history.
Archaeologists date a find by the layer it sits in and the clues it holds.
Coins point to King David, and an inscription names Pontius Pilate.
challenges: Ask someone older to show you a family keepsake and tell its story.
Notice clues in everyday objects that reveal when they were made.
Read a Bible story this week as an account of real people and places.

questions: Could Jesus fulfilling so many prophecies really be just coincidence?
What hard question about Jesus or the Bible have you been holding back?
Why was a spiritual kingdom so hard to accept for people expecting a ruler?
takeaways: If the Bible is trustworthy history, its prophecy deserves a serious look.
Many expected a political ruler, but Jesus brought a spiritual kingdom.
Following Jesus as Messiah can mean a whole shift in how you see the world.
challenges: Write down your questions about prophecy and bring them to club next week.
Read Isaiah 52 and 53 and note what they say about the coming Messiah.
Ask yourself which of your expectations Jesus might turn upside down.

questions: If the Bible really is all we've said it is, what changes for you now?
How would you answer "men wrote the Bible, so how can it be God's word?"
What from the last four weeks most changed how you see the Bible, and why?
takeaways: If the Bible is truly God's word, it has real authority over how we live.
As Jesus is fully man and fully God, the Bible is from men and from God.
The Bible shows who God really is, not just what people thought about him.
challenges: Make time this week to read more of the Bible than you usually do.
Write down one thing the Bible teaches and actually follow it this week.
Practice explaining to a friend why you believe the Bible has authority.

questions: When have you felt lost, and what finally helped you find your way?
Does calling evil the absence of good change how you see it? Why?
What question about suffering do you most wish you could ask God?
takeaways: Evil is not a thing God made; it is the absence of good, like darkness.
Evil entered the world when we chose to push God out of the picture.
The very existence of evil points to a real standard: God exists.
challenges: Notice something you call evil this week and ask what good it lacks.
Write down one hard question about suffering to bring back next week.
Notice this week when you use yourself as your compass instead of God.

questions: If God is all-powerful, is there anything He still cannot do?
Why doesn't a God who can speak a universe into being just stop all evil?
What good have you ever seen come out of something painful or hard?
takeaways: God did not create evil, and He is not responsible for it.
God cannot lie or contradict Himself, even though He is all-powerful.
God has good reasons for allowing evil for a time; we only see in part now.
challenges: Write down a few things God cannot do and what each shows about who He is.
When you see evil this week, look to God for hope instead of doubting Him.
Think of a time a parent's hard rule turned out to be for your good.

questions: When you are hurting, which of the video's questions do you ask God most?
How did the lepers see Father Damien differently once he said "we lepers"?
Does knowing Jesus felt betrayal and physical pain change how you pray?
takeaways: God is not distant from our pain; in Jesus he came and suffered with us.
The cross is Christianity's symbol: a God who knows suffering firsthand.
Because Jesus is risen, suffering and death do not get the final word.
challenges: Name one pain you carry and tell God honestly whether you will trust him.
Like Father Damien, step toward someone who is suffering this week.
Reread Joseph's story and notice how God turned evil into good.

questions: If your favorite place lost every good thing, what would be left?
If God is good and allows suffering, how can hell fit with that?
Why does it matter whether God sends people to hell or we send ourselves?
takeaways: Hell is not God; it is the tragic consequence of rejecting Him.
Every breath, sunny day, and rainfall is God's common grace to everyone.
God invites us into relationship but never forces us; that is love.
challenges: Take stock of where you stand with God now versus the start of the year.
Each day, notice one gift God gives you whether you choose Him or not.
Bring your honest questions about hell to small group; don't hide them.

questions: When you think of a time you truly felt loved, what did it feel like?
When you share your faith, do you want to be right or to love?
How could you show someone Jesus by the way you listen to them?
takeaways: Paul says all our knowledge is worth nothing without love.
Sharing your faith is about building relationships, not winning.
The way you love others may be the only way some ever see Jesus.
challenges: Have one real conversation this week where you listen more than you talk.
Practice explaining what you believe with humility, not to win.
If a conversation goes badly, learn from it and try again next time.

questions: What makes starting a spiritual conversation feel scary to you?
Why do we feel we need all the answers before sharing our faith?
Someone says there is too much evil for God to exist; what would you ask?
takeaways: You do not need every answer to have a real conversation about Jesus.
Asking 'What do you mean by that?' digs deeper and buys you time to think.
Good questions show love and build the relationship discipleship needs.
challenges: Ask someone 'How did you come to that conclusion?' and really listen.
Notice when you reach for a quick comeback and ask a question instead.
Have a face-to-face conversation this week asking real why questions.

questions: Have you ever been told to just believe when you wanted real answers?
Why might learning more about your faith lead to even more questions?
Does hearing that others have doubts too make it easier to share yours?
takeaways: Doubts that never get answered are one reason people walk away from faith.
Asking hard questions can actually make your faith stronger, not weaker.
God can handle any doubt; He has given you all you need to be confident.
challenges: Write down one question you are wrestling with and bring it to your leader.
When a doubt comes up this week, talk about it instead of hiding it.
Ask someone older how they made it through a season of doubt.

questions: Look back at your notes from lesson one: how has your thinking changed?
Which of your early questions about faith got answered, and which remain?
What part could you play in helping a friend come to know Jesus?
takeaways: It is not our job to save anyone; God alone causes the growth.
Falling flat while sharing the gospel often teaches more than success does.
God gifts each of us differently, so be faithful with what you were given.
challenges: Reread your notes from the start of the year and write down what changed.
Write down one question you still have and decide where to seek the answer.
Take one step of sharing the truth this week, even if it goes badly.
